# Bayesian inference and Bayesian statistics

A full university course, written for advanced undergraduates, MSc and PhD students, and anyone with the background to work through it alone. Thirty-two chapters run from measure-theoretic foundations to modern probabilistic workflow, with derivations worked in full, runnable labs in `R`, `Stan`, and `JAX`, and exercises throughout.

The premise: Bayesian statistics is a workflow, not a formula. It starts with a probability model, passes through prior specification and posterior computation, and ends in decision-relevant summaries, predictive checks, and criticism of the model you just fitted [@bernardo1994; @gelman2013; @gelman2020].

[Start here](teaching-philosophy.qmd) · [Install the tools](appendix/software-setup.qmd) · [Schedule](syllabus.qmd)
:::

## The course

::: {.grid-cards}
::: {.course-card}
### [I. Foundations](parts/part-i-foundations.qmd)
Probability spaces, conditional expectation, limit theorems, likelihood theory, Bayes' theorem, exchangeability.
:::

::: {.course-card}
### [II. Core inference](parts/part-ii-core-bayesian-inference.qmd)
Conjugate analysis, marginal likelihoods, decision theory, prior design and sensitivity.
:::

::: {.course-card}
### [III. Computation](parts/part-iii-computation.qmd)
Laplace approximation, Monte Carlo, MCMC, HMC and NUTS, variational inference, particle methods, the telescoping sampler.
:::

::: {.course-card}
### [IV. Models](parts/part-iv-models.qmd)
Linear models, GLMs, hierarchical models, mixtures, state-space models, Gaussian processes, spatial and causal models.
:::

::: {.course-card}
### [V. Diagnostics](parts/part-v-optimization-and-diagnostics.qmd)
MAP estimation, tuning and calibration, convergence diagnostics, posterior predictive checking.
:::

::: {.course-card}
### [VI. Software](parts/part-vi-software-workflows.qmd)
End-to-end workflows in `R`, `Stan`, and `JAX`, with reproducibility treated as part of the analysis.
:::

::: {.course-card}
### [VII. Advanced](parts/part-vii-advanced-topics.qmd)
Model selection and stacking, robustness, experimental design, communication, capstone work.
:::
:::

## Where to start

::: {.panel-tabset}
### I know some statistics

Skim [Part I](parts/part-i-foundations.qmd) and begin at [conjugate analysis](chapters/core/conjugate-analysis.qmd). Come back to the measure-theoretic material when a proof depends on it.

Then follow the main line: [Bayesian linear models](chapters/models/bayesian-linear-models.qmd) → [hierarchical models](chapters/models/hierarchical-and-multilevel-models.qmd) → [MCMC](chapters/computation/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd) → [diagnostics](chapters/practice/diagnostics-and-model-criticism.qmd).

### I'm an applied statistician

Start with [conjugate analysis](chapters/core/conjugate-analysis.qmd) and [Bayesian linear models](chapters/models/bayesian-linear-models.qmd), then go straight to the [workflow chapters](parts/part-vi-software-workflows.qmd) and fit something.

Return to [Part I](parts/part-i-foundations.qmd) once the practice has given the theory something to attach to. Most people find it easier in that order.

### I implement algorithms

Pair [Part III](parts/part-iii-computation.qmd) with the [JAX chapter](chapters/software/jax-gradient-based-bayes.qmd), writing each sampler by hand before using a library version.

[The telescoping sampler](chapters/computation/telescoping-sampler.qmd) and the [funnel geometry](chapters/models/hierarchical-and-multilevel-models.qmd) are the two places where implementation detail genuinely changes the statistics.

### I'm just looking

Read [hierarchical and multilevel models](chapters/models/hierarchical-and-multilevel-models.qmd). It has the derivations, the decision-theoretic argument, the geometry, and a worked example, so it shows the intended depth better than any description would.
:::

## What you need

Multivariable calculus, linear algebra to the level of eigenvalues and quadratic forms, undergraduate probability and statistics, and basic `R` or `Python`. No prior exposure to Bayesian methods.

The appendices cover [notation](appendix/notation.qmd), a [measure-theoretic refresher](appendix/measure-probability-review.qmd), and [installation](appendix/software-setup.qmd).

## Three tools, three purposes

The same model, three ways — this is the eight schools hierarchical model that runs through the course.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### `R`

Simulation, conjugate calculations, custom samplers, and posterior summaries [@r2025; @posterior2024].

```r
# Partial pooling by hand: the shrinkage factor is the whole idea.
B <- sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + tau^2)
theta_hat <- (1 - B) * y + B * mu
```

### `Stan`

A mature HMC and NUTS implementation, for hierarchical and nonlinear models [@carpenter2017; @hoffman2014].

```stan
parameters {
  real mu;
  real<lower=0> tau;
  vector[J] z;                      // standardised group effects
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[J] theta = mu + tau * z;   // non-centring: no funnel here
}
model {
  z ~ std_normal();
  y ~ normal(theta, sigma);
}
```

### `JAX`

Automatic differentiation and JIT, for chapters where the point is to build the algorithm rather than call it [@jax2018].

```python
# Writing HMC by hand is the fastest way to see what Stan does for you.
grad_logp = jax.grad(log_posterior)
p -= 0.5 * eps * -grad_logp(q)     # leapfrog half-step
q += eps * p
```
:::

Every lab in the repository runs: `R` in `labs/r/`, Stan in `labs/stan/`, Python in `labs/jax/`.
